label: Attached Foraminifera form plane spirals with whorls flattened on the attached side
statement: Most spiral Foraminifera are plane (discoid) spirals because some force keeps the chambers in a plane, especially in forms that live attached to rock or seaweed, whose whorls are flattened on the attached surface; freely floating forms such as Globigerina tend towards helicoid spirals.
quote: The majority of spiral forms, on the other hand, are plane or discoid spirals, and we may take it that in these cases some force has exercised a controlling influence, so as to keep all the chambers in a plane. This is especially the case in forms like Rotalia or Discorbina (Fig. 316), where the organism lives attached to a rock or a frond of sea-weed

label: Many foraminiferal species and genera may be temporary manifestations of variability
statement: Because very slight changes in surface energies could turn one foraminiferal form into another, many forms distinguished as separate species and even genera may be no more than temporary manifestations of variability, as in Peneroplis.
quote: but for all we know of the life-history of the Foraminifera, it may well be that a great number of the other forms which we distinguish as separate species and even genera are no more than temporary manifestations of the same variability

label: Foraminiferal forms follow such simple laws that none is fitter than another to survive
statement: Foraminiferal shells grow by laws so simple and so in harmony with their material and the forces acting on them that no form is better, fitter or less fit to survive than another, which accounts for the great diversity of types and their persistence since the Cretaceous.
quote: It leads one to imagine that these shells have grown according to laws so simple, so much in harmony with their material, with their environment, and with all the forces internal and external to which they are exposed, that none is better than another and none fitter or less fit to survive.

label: Identical foraminiferal forms may have arisen independently again and again
statement: The possible lines of variation in Foraminifera may be so narrow and determinate that identical forms have arisen independently many times.
quote: It invites one also to contemplate the possibility of the lines of possible variation being here so narrow and determinate that identical forms may have come independently into being again and again.

label: Increased shell strength is not an advantage driving foraminiferal evolution
statement: Against Rhumbler, niceties of shell form have little effect on survival: delicate foraminiferal shells survive unbroken in vast numbers, so breakage is not a constant danger and increased strength is not a selective advantage guiding their evolution.
quote: And so I am not inclined to believe that niceties of form affect the case very much: nor in general that foraminiferal life involves a struggle for existence wherein breakage is a constant danger to be averted, and increased strength an advantage to be ensured.

label: Foraminifera are absent from coarse gravels because of hydraulic sorting by currents
statement: Foraminiferal shells are absent from coarse sands and gravels not because they avoid concussion but because light shells are sorted by currents like any other graded sediment, settling where water is still.
quote: The coarseness or fineness of the sediment on the sea-bottom is a measure of the current: where the current is strong the larger stones are washed clean, where there is perfect stillness the finest mud settles down; and the light, fragile shells of the Foraminifera find their appropriate place, like every other graded sediment, in this spontaneous order of lixiviation.

label: Forms set by physical forces undermine inference of kinship from similarity
statement: Insofar as forms depend on physical forces and their variations on simple quantitative changes in those forces, similarity of form cannot safely be taken as evidence of consanguinity, and the link between classification and phylogeny must be revised.
quote: But in so far as forms can be shewn to depend on the play of physical forces, and the variations of form to be directly due to simple quantitative variations in these, just so far are we thrown back on our guard before the biological conception of consanguinity, and compelled to revise the vague canons which connect classification with phylogeny.
scope: Foraminifera and other organisms whose form is governed by physical forces

label: Rhinoceros horn is a plane logarithmic spiral from constant front-to-back growth ratio
statement: The rhinoceros horn grows faster anteriorly than posteriorly in a constant ratio, so it curves as a logarithmic spiral; lying in the median plane, it has no lateral twist and forms a plane spiral.
quote: Its longitudinal growth proceeds with a maximum velocity anteriorly, and a minimum posteriorly; and the ratio of these velocities being constant, the horn curves into the form of a logarithmic spiral in the manner that we have already studied.

label: Paired horns of ruminants are conjugate, mirror-image spirals
statement: The paired horns of hollow-horned ruminants are conjugate spirals, the left horn being the mirror image of the right.
quote: But the two horns are in symmetry one with another; they form “conjugate” spirals, one being the “mirror-image” of the other.

label: Most horns are logarithmic spirals from constant unequal growth on opposite sides
statement: In the great majority of horns the curve is a continuous logarithmic spiral, caused by unequal rates of growth parallel to the axis on opposite sides of the horn, the inequality keeping a constant ratio throughout growth.
quote: But in the great majority of horns, we have no difficulty in recognising a continuous logarithmic spiral, nor in referring it, as before, to an unequal rate of growth (parallel to the axis) on two opposite sides of the horn, the inequality maintaining a constant ratio as long as growth proceeds.

label: Goat and sheep horns form a series of homologous spirals of increasing angle
statement: Horns of wild goats and sheep form a series of homologous logarithmic spirals with increasing constant angle: under 40° in Oryx, under 70° in the Scinde wild goat, about 75° in Ovis ammon and a little more in the Highland ram.
quote: we may easily arrange a series of forms, such for example as the Siberian ibex, the moufflon, _Ovis Ammon_, etc., and ending with the long-horned Highland ram: in which, as we pass from one to another, we recognise precisely homologous spirals, with an increasing angular constant, the spiral angle being, for instance, about 75° or rather less in _Ovis Ammon_, and in the Highland ram a very little more.
scope: horns of Oryx, Capra and Ovis species

label: Argali horns share a spiral angle but differ in their shearing (helical) component
statement: Among closely allied wild sheep (Argali) the constant angle of the horn's logarithmic spiral is nearly the same, and the species differ chiefly in the helical shearing component.
quote: In all of these the constant angle of the logarithmic spiral is very much the same, but the shearing component differs greatly.
scope: Asiatic wild sheep (Ovis ammon, O. poli, O. hodgsoni)

label: A horn is a plane spiral only if fastest and slowest growth lie diametrically opposite
statement: If the maximal and minimal growth rates around the basal growth zone of a horn lie diametrically opposite, the horn is a plane spiral; otherwise it is a spiral in space with a helical component, which is the usual case because the horn's field of force has no such plane of symmetry.
quote: If the maximal and minimal velocities of growth be precisely at opposite sides of the zone of growth, the resultant spiral will be a plane spiral; but if they be not precisely or diametrically opposite, then the spiral will be a spiral in space, with a winding or helical component

label: Uneven adhesion of the horn sheath to its bony core can itself produce the spiral
statement: Unequal retardation of the growing horn sheath by its adhesion to the bony core can produce the same spiral as unequal growth, and is probably a very important and sometimes the chief factor in horn curvature.
quote: had its elongation more retarded on one side than the other (prior to its complete solidification) by varying degrees of adhesion or membranous attachment to the bone core within, then the net result would be a spiral curve precisely such as would have arisen from initial inequalities in the rate of growth itself. It seems highly probable that this is a very important factor

label: The thicker the horn, the greater its spiral curvature
statement: On the whole, thicker horns are more strongly spirally curved than slender ones, because a larger cross-section allows greater differences in growth or retardation between opposite sides.
quote: I think it may be said that, on the whole, the thicker the horn, the greater is its spiral curvature.
scope: horns of antelopes, goats and sheep

label: Sinuous growth lines on non-cylindrical horns result from torsional strain
statement: Horns that grow as curves of double curvature undergo torsional strain, because the sheath is attached to the core, and this strain warps the rings into the sinuous growth lines predicted by St Venant for a twisted non-circular prism; such lines are absent from cylindrical ox horns.
quote: But there is yet another and a very remarkable phenomenon which we may discern in the growth of a horn, when it takes the form of a curve of double curvature, namely, an effect of torsional strain; and this it is which gives rise to the sinuous “lines of growth,” or sinuous boundaries of the separate horny rings, of which we have already spoken.
scope: horns of sheep, Ovis ammon, antelopes; contrasted with oxen

label: Twining of climbing stems results from unequal growth on different sides
statement: The revolving nutation of twining plants, like the helicoid growth of an antelope horn, is caused by unequal rates of growth on different sides of the stem, the difference being that in the stem growth occurs along its whole length.
quote: This tendency to revolution—“circumvolution,” as Darwin calls it, “revolving nutation,” as Sachs puts it—is very closely comparable to the process by which an antelope’s horn (such as the koodoo’s) grows into its spiral or rather helicoid form; and it is simply due, in like manner, to inequalities in the rate of growth on different sides of the growing stem.

label: Stem torsion on rough supports is a mechanical couple from adhesion, not an adaptation
statement: Twining stems become twisted on rough supports but not on smooth ones because adhesion to the rough support sets up a mechanical couple, so Darwin's adaptive explanation (gaining rigidity) is unnecessary.
quote: In the case of the roughened support, there is a temporary adhesion or “clinging” between it and the growing stem which twines around it; and a system of forces is thus set up, producing a “couple,” just as it was in the case of the ram’s or antelope’s horn through direct adhesion of the bony core to the surrounding sheath.

label: A pair of antlers is confined to a single smooth spheroidal surface
statement: The branches of a pair of deer antlers are confined to a single, more or less spheroidal or ellipsoidal curved surface, the two antlers forming one mirror-symmetric surface whose tine tips lie on a continuous curve; the antler is essentially a surface, whereas a horn is an axial rod.
quote: The surface to which the branches of the antler tend to be confined is a more or less spheroidal, or occasionally an ellipsoidal one; and furthermore, when we inspect any well-developed pair of antlers, such as those of a red deer, a sambur or a wapiti, we have no difficulty in seeing that the two antlers make up between them _a single surface_

label: Claws, beaks and teeth grown by unequal permanent accretion are logarithmic spirals
statement: Wherever a structure grows by permanent increments with unequal longitudinal growth about its axis, as in nails, claws, beaks and teeth, it always tends to the form of a logarithmic spiral, which becomes conspicuous only when the structure is long.
quote: The logarithmic spiral _always_ tends to manifest itself in such structures as these, though it usually only attracts our attention in elongated structures, where (that is to say) the radius vector has described a considerable angle.
scope: nails, claws, beaks, incisors, canines and tusks of vertebrates

label: Elephant and American mastodon tusks are the same spiral as the mammoth's, only shorter
statement: The tusks of living elephants and American mastodons follow essentially the same logarithmic spiral as the mammoth's great spiral tusks and differ only in size, so that if they grew long enough they would become equally spiral.
quote: but the American mastodons and the existing species of elephant have tusks which do not differ appreciably, except in size, from the great spiral tusks of the mammoth, though from their comparative shortness the spiral is little developed and only appears to the eye as a gentle curve.
scope: tusks of elephants, mastodons and mammoths (Proboscidea)

label: Spirals of sunflower, thistle and cone are deformations of helices on a stem
statement: The logarithmic spirals of flat or convex inflorescences and the helices on elongated stems are one phenomenon: the fir-cone, teasel, thistle and sunflower heads are successive geometric deformations of a long, nearly cylindrical stem, on which the same arrangement appears as helices.
quote: The fir-cone may be looked upon as a cylindrical axis contracted at both ends, until it becomes approximately an ellipsoidal solid of revolution, generated about the long axis of the ellipse; and the semi-ellipsoidal capitulum of the teasel, the more or less hemispherical one of the thistle, and the flattened but still convex one of the sunflower, are all beautiful and successive deformations of what is typically a long, conical, and all but cylindrical stem.
scope: leaf, scale and floret arrangements in plants

label: Phyllotactic spirals follow inevitably from similar parts produced at regular intervals
statement: There is no subtle mystery in phyllotaxis: the steady production of similar parts, similarly placed, at similar successive intervals of time necessarily produces symmetrical patterns (helices on a cylinder, logarithmic spirals on a surface containing the pole), which are a secondary mathematical result rather than a primary phenomenon.
quote: I, for my part, see no subtle mystery in the matter, other than what lies in the steady production of similar growing parts, similarly situated, at similar successive intervals of time.
scope: phyllotaxis of leaves, florets, bracts and scales

label: Sunflower spirals intersect isogonally, rarely orthogonally
statement: Against Church, the spirals in a sunflower disc intersect isogonally (at a constant angle), and orthogonal intersection is only a particular and probably infrequent case.
quote: The spirals intersect isogonally, but orthogonal intersection would be only one particular case, and in all probability a very infrequent one, in the intersection of logarithmic spirals developed about a common pole.
scope: parastichies in sunflower capitula and similar inflorescences

label: Parastichy counts on fir-cones are nearly constant within a species
statement: The numbers of conspicuous parastichies on fir-cones are on the whole very constant within a species, e.g. 5 and 3 in the Norway spruce and 8 and 5 in the common larch.
quote: and among fir-cones, we can easily count these, and we find them to be on the whole very constant in number, according to the species.

label: Parastichy numbers change when the structure varies greatly in size
statement: Phyllotactic parastichy numbers vary with the size of the whole structure, as in sunflower discs where one species may show 34/55, 55/89 or even 89/144 rows.
quote: The arrangement, as we have seen, is apt to vary when the entire structure varies greatly in size, as in the disc of the sunflower.
scope: sunflower capitula and other composite inflorescences

label: Right- and left-handed parastichy directions occur about equally often
statement: Within a species, cones with a given parastichy arrangement are nearly equally divided between right-handed and left-handed spiral directions (e.g. 224 versus 243 among 467 Norway spruce cones).
quote: In each case they were nearly equally divided as regards direction; for instance of the 467 cones shewing the five-eight arrangement, the five-series ran in right-handed spirals in 224 cases, and in left-handed spirals in 243.
scope: conifer cones (Norway spruce) and phyllotactic systems generally

label: One Fibonacci parastichy pair necessarily entails all the lower pairs
statement: Following Tait, if a single genetic spiral exists and one pair of parastichy numbers from the series 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13… is present, all the lower pairs of the series are necessarily present in the same system.
quote: These are the very series which we have found to be common, or normal; and so far as our investigation has yet gone, it has proved to us that, if one of these exists, it entails, _ipso facto_, the presence of the rest.
scope: spiral phyllotactic systems with a single genetic spiral

label: Most phyllotaxis has between two and three leaves per turn of the genetic spiral
statement: The prevalence of Fibonacci parastichy numbers arises because in the great majority of fir-cones and other phyllotactic systems there are more than two but fewer than three leaves in one turn of the genetic spiral (t = 2); other observed series correspond to t = 3, 4, 5.
quote: And, determined in this manner, it is found in the great majority of cases, in fir-cones and a host of other examples of phyllotaxis, that _t_ = 2.

label: Which parastichies are conspicuous depends on leaf proportions, not on divergence
statement: Which of the implicit spiral families is conspicuous does not depend on the angle of divergence but on the proportions of the leaves or scales, strictly on the ratio of the diagonals of the rhomboid circumscribing each leaf-area.
quote: the conspicuousness of one set or another does not depend upon angular divergence. It depends on the relative proportions in length and breadth of the leaves themselves; or, more strictly speaking, on the ratio of the diagonals of the rhomboidal figure by which each leaf-area is circumscribed.

label: Convergence of phyllotactic ratios to the golden mean has no biological significance
statement: That the phyllotactic fractions 1/2, 2/3, 3/5… converge to 0.618…, the golden mean, is a mathematical coincidence without biological significance; the precise divergence angle and orthostichies are likewise unimportant.
quote: And lastly, the fact that the successional numbers, expressed as fractions, 1/2, 2/3, 3/5, represent a convergent series, whose final term is equal to 0·61803..., the _sectio aurea_ or “golden mean” of unity, is seen to be a mathematical coincidence, devoid of biological significance

label: Close approximations to the golden mean are rare; poor ones like 2/3 are common
statement: Against the 'ideal angle' theory, phyllotactic arrangements that closely approximate the golden mean (8/13, 13/21, 34/55 and higher) are comparatively rare, while poorer approximations such as 3/5, 2/3 and 1/2 are extremely common.
quote: the arrangements by which a better approximation is got, such as 8/13, 13/21, and the very close approximations such as 34/55, 55/89, 89/144, etc., are comparatively rare, while the much less close approximations of 3/5 or 2/3, or even 1/2, are extremely common.

label: Leaf exposure is changed far more by internode length than by divergence angle
statement: If leaves benefit from being spread apart for exposure to air, lengthening the axis to separate them vertically has a far greater effect than any adjustment of the divergence angle, so the azimuthal 'ideal angle' cannot be the plant's means of optimising exposure.
quote: then it is surely manifest that the simple way to do so is to elongate the axis, and to set the leaves further apart, lengthways on the stem. This has at once a far more potent effect than any nice manipulation of the “angle of divergence.”

label: The Fibonacci series has no adaptive role introduced by natural selection
statement: The Fibonacci series in phyllotaxis, its supposed usefulness, and the hypothesis that natural selection introduced it into plant structure have no place in the study of botanical phenomena.
quote: We come then, without more ado, to the conclusion that the “Fibonacci series,” and its supposed usefulness, and the hypothesis of its introduction into plant-structure through natural selection, are all matters which deserve no place in the plain study of botanical phenomena.

label: Eggs are prolate spheroids, never oblate
statement: Hard-shelled eggs, while often pointed, are never flattened or discoidal: they are prolate, never oblate, solids of revolution.
quote: It is an obvious but by no means negligible fact that the egg, while often pointed, is never flattened or discoidal; it is a prolate, but never an oblate, spheroid.
scope: eggs of birds, tortoises and crocodiles

label: Egg shape is caused by radial pressure of the oviduct before the shell hardens
statement: The essential cause of the form and variation of form of an egg is the regularly varying, largely radial pressure applied by successive rings of the oviduct before the shell solidifies, not adaptation to nesting circumstances.
quote: this factor, the unknown but regularly varying, largely radial, pressure applied by successive annuli of the oviduct, is the essential cause of the form, and variations of form, of the egg.
scope: birds' eggs and other hard-shelled eggs

label: The most pointed eggs are those largest relative to the parent bird
statement: As a very common rule, the most asymmetrical, posteriorly tapered eggs are those that are large relative to the parent bird (guillemot, curlews, sandpipers, terns), because they are under the greatest pressure in the oviduct; relatively large but symmetrical eggs (apteryx) imply a relatively large oviduct.
quote: It can be shown, at least as a very common rule, that those eggs which are most unsymmetrical, or most tapered off posteriorly, are also eggs of a large size relatively to the parent bird.

label: A pullet's first eggs are smaller and rounder than its later ones
statement: In the domestic fowl egg size and shape are directly related: a young pullet's first eggs are smaller and more nearly spherical than later ones, and breeds laying relatively smaller eggs lay rounder eggs.
quote: In the case of the common fowl we can trace a direct relation between the size and shape of the egg, for the first eggs laid by a young pullet are usually smaller, and at the same time are much more nearly spherical than the later ones

label: Peristaltic pressure behind the egg's middle makes the front blunt and rear pointed
statement: Peristaltic contraction of the oviduct applies greatest pressure behind the middle of the forming egg, making the anterior end broader and the posterior narrower; the resulting tapered form also favours movement down the oviduct blunt end first.
quote: from the nature and direction of motion of the peristaltic wave the pressure will be greatest somewhere behind the middle of the egg; in other words, the tube is converted for the time being into a more conical form, and the simple result follows that the anterior end of the egg becomes the broader and the posterior end the narrower.

label: Egg form obeys p_n + T(1/r + 1/r′) = P, the equation of all eggs
statement: The shape of an egg, as an extensible membrane filled with incompressible fluid under external pressure, obeys p_n + T(1/r + 1/r′) = P (external normal pressure plus membrane tension times total curvature equals internal pressure), which Thompson calls the equation of all eggs.
quote: In fact, in so far as the postulates correspond near enough to actualities, the above equation is the equation of _all eggs_ in the universe.

label: Membrane tension peaks at the small end, where abnormal eggs are irregular
statement: In conical eggs with spherical ends, the tension of the envelope is greatest at and near the small end, so that is where eggs are most likely to be distorted or to burst and where abnormal eggs most often show irregularities.
quote: further, that the tension _T_ is greatest at and near the small end of the egg. It is here, in short, that the egg is most likely to be irregularly distorted or even to burst, and it is here that we most commonly find irregularities of shape in abnormal eggs.
scope: birds' eggs, especially pointed eggs and abnormal hen's eggs

label: Lateral spine of Schistosoma eggs is moulded in the ootype, not a species mark
statement: Following Looss, the lateral spine of some Schistosoma eggs is moulded mechanically in a funnel-shaped part of the uterus, so lateral- and terminal-spined eggs are mechanical variants of one thing and do not show the existence of a separate species, S. mansoni.
quote: It ascribes to a mechanical cause a curious peculiarity of form; it shews, by reference to this mechanical principle, that two conditions which were very different to the systematic naturalist’s eye, were really only two simple mechanical modifications of the same thing; and it destroys the chief evidence for the existence of a supposed new species of worm
scope: eggs of Schistosoma haematobium and S. mansoni

label: Sea-urchin shell outlines match liquid drops flattened by gravity
statement: The vertical outlines of regular sea-urchin shells are the forms of liquid drops depressed by gravity (with the pull of the tube-feet), their degree of flattening varying with the tension or strength of the shell: strong shells (Palaeechinus) stay nearly spherical, soft flexible ones (Phormosoma) are most flattened.
quote: but we have no difficulty in seeing that the various forms represented in a series of sea-urchin shells are no other than those which we may easily and perfectly imitate in drops.

label: Vessel wall thickness tracks radius in large arteries but falls off in small ones
statement: Under constant pressure the wall thickness of a blood-vessel should vary as its radius (P = T/R); because pressure falls with friction from large to small arteries, wall thickness is proportional to vessel size in larger vessels but becomes disproportionately thin in small arteries and capillaries.
quote: and accordingly we find that while, for a time, the cross-sections of the larger and smaller vessels are symmetrical figures, with the wall-thickness proportional to the size of the tube, this proportion is gradually lost, and the walls of the small arteries, and still more of the capillaries, become exceedingly thin, and more so than in strict proportion to the narrowing of the tube.

label: Heart wall thickness varies inversely with the mean curvature of the chamber
statement: Within each cavity of the heart, where pressure is uniform, wall thickness t varies inversely as the mean curvature, t(1/r + 1/r′) = C, so the highly curved apex of the left ventricle is thinnest.
quote: that is to say, that the thickness (_t_) of the wall varies inversely as the mean curvature.

label: Left ventricle wall is 6–7 times right's, matching the pressure ratio
statement: The left ventricle requires six to seven times the dilating pressure of the right, and its wall thickness is greater in the same proportion.
quote: we find (1) that we have had to use a pressure in the left ventricle from six to seven times as great as in the right ventricle, and (2) that the thickness of the walls is just in the same proportion.

label: Blood-vessels are arranged for minimum effort and minimum wall-surface
statement: The form and arrangement of blood-vessels are such that circulation proceeds with a minimum of effort and a minimum of wall-surface (and hence of friction).
quote: The general principle is that the form and arrangement of the blood-vessels is such that the circulation proceeds with a minimum of effort, and with a minimum of wall-surface, the latter condition leading to a minimum of friction and being therefore included in the first.

label: Small arterial branches leave at large angles, large branches at small angles
statement: Small arterial branches come off the main stem at large angles (about 70°–90° for the smallest) and large branches at small angles, with equal branches diverging at equal angles, as Roux's rules state.
quote: In other words, it would seem that for small branches a large angle of bifurcation, and for large branches a small one, is always the better.

label: Optimal branching angle has cosine equal to ratio of energy loss in trunk and branch
statement: The most favourable angle at which an arterial branch leaves its trunk is that whose cosine equals the ratio of energy loss per unit length in the main vessel to that in the branch (cos x = L/L′).
quote: That is to say, the most favourable angle of branching will be such that the cosine of the angle is equal to the ratio of the loss of energy which the blood undergoes, per unit of length, in the main vessel, as compared with that which it undergoes in the branch.

label: Mechanical adaptations of form are demonstrable, unlike colour adaptations
statement: Unlike explanations of colouration as cryptic, warning or mimetic, which cannot be demonstrated, the fitness of organic form for mechanical functions such as swimming or flight can be analysed and established in detail by statics and dynamics.
quote: But of a very different order from all such “adaptations” as these, are those very perfect adaptations of form which, for instance, fit a fish for swimming or a bird for flight. Here we are far above the region of mere hypothesis, for we have to deal with questions of mechanical efficiency where statical and dynamical considerations can be applied and established in detail.
scope: adaptive form and colouration of animals in general

label: Bone is nearly as strong in tension as in compression
statement: Fresh bone resists tearing almost as well as it resists crushing (tensile strength about 9–12 and crushing strength about 13–16 kg per sq. mm), which makes it an economical structural material that can serve equally as tie or strut.
quote: At first sight, bone seems weak indeed; but it has the great and unusual advantage that it is very nearly as good for a tie as for a strut, nearly as strong to withstand rupture, or tearing asunder, as to resist crushing.

label: Structures that must resist bending are built as hollow tubes
statement: Where stiffness against bending in all directions is required, organisms use a hollow cylindrical construction with little or no material in the core, as in the thin-walled, almost empty wing bones of long-winged birds such as the albatross, quills, and hollow stems of reeds and straw.
quote: And it is not only in the supporting pillar that such a construction is useful; it is appropriate in every case where _stiffness_ is required, where bending has to be resisted. The long bone of a bird’s wing has little or no weight to carry, but it has to withstand powerful bending moments; and in the arm-bone of a long-winged bird, such as an albatross, we see the tubular construction manifested in its perfection
scope: long bones of vertebrates (especially bird wing bones), feather quills and cylindrical plant stems

label: Femoral wall thickness follows the bending-moment distribution along the shaft
statement: Because bending strain is greatest at mid-length of a bent column, the walls of a long bone such as the femur are thickest in the middle of the shaft and thin gradually towards the ends, so that wall thickness forms a graph of the bending moments along the bone.
quote: Hence, if our cylindrical column be exposed to strong bending stresses, it will be prudent and economical to make its walls thickest in the middle and thinning off gradually towards the ends; and if we look at a longitudinal section of a thigh-bone, we shall see that this is just what nature has done.
scope: weight-bearing long bones, especially the human femur

label: Trabeculae of cancellous bone follow the lines of compressive and tensile stress
statement: The trabeculae of cancellous bone, as in the head of the femur, are arranged along the principal lines of compressive and tensile stress of the loaded bone, crossing one another at right angles, exactly as in the engineer's stress diagram of a comparable structure such as a crane-head.
quote: and we have no difficulty in seeing that the anatomical arrangement of the trabeculae follows precisely the mechanical distribution of compressive and tensile stress or, in other words, accords perfectly with the theoretical stress-diagram of the crane.
scope: cancellous bone of weight-bearing vertebrate bones (femur, tibia, calcaneus)

label: Shear removes obliquely laid trabeculae, leaving those aligned with stress lines
statement: Trabecular alignment arises because a trabecula laid down along a pressure or tension line is undisturbed, since there is no shear along those lines, whereas one lying obliquely is acted on by shearing force and displaced until it comes into line with the stress.
quote: If it lie in the direction of one of the pressure-lines, for instance, it will be in a position of comparative equilibrium, or minimal disturbance; but if it be inclined obliquely to the pressure-lines, the shearing force will at once tend to act upon it and move it away.
scope: formation of trabecular bone (and by extension fibre alignment in plants)

label: Trabecular architecture remodels to new force patterns after malunited fracture
statement: Trabecular arrangement is produced by the forces acting on the bone, not by heredity: when a fracture heals with the parts displaced so that the stress lines are redistributed, the trabecular system is entirely remodelled within weeks to align with the new forces, even at a distance from the injury.
quote: If a bone be broken and so repaired that its parts lie somewhat out of their former place, so that the pressure-and tension-lines have now a new distribution, before many weeks are over the trabecular system will be found to have been entirely remodelled, so as to fall into line with the new system of forces.
scope: living vertebrate bone after fracture, malunion or transplantation

label: Mechanical strain directly stimulates growth
statement: A state of strain produced by stress is a direct stimulus to growth, so that tissues under increased load grow stronger or thicker, as when the fibula of a puppy whose tibia was excised grew as thick as or thicker than the normal tibia.
quote: a condition of _strain_, the result of a _stress_, is a direct stimulus to growth itself. This indeed is no less than one of the cardinal facts of theoretical biology.
scope: living tissues of animals and plants, especially bone, skin and supporting plant tissues

label: The quadruped backbone is a double-armed cantilever girder, not an arch
statement: Because the jointed legs cannot resist the horizontal thrust of an arch and there is no tie between its ends, the backbone of a standing quadruped is not an arch, tied arch or bowstring girder but is mechanically comparable to the main girder of a double-armed cantilever bridge.
quote: The structure is not an arch, nor a tied arch, nor a bowstring girder: but it is strictly and beautifully comparable to the main girder of a double-armed cantilever bridge.
scope: vertebral column and associated ligaments of standing quadrupeds

label: Quadrupeds carry more of their weight on the fore-legs than on the hind-legs
statement: In large quadrupeds the fore-legs carry considerably more of the body weight than the hind-legs (about 55–58% in horses and elephants and about two-thirds in camels and llamas).
quote: It will be observed that in all these animals the load upon the fore-feet preponderates considerably over that upon the hind, the preponderance being rather greater in the elephant than in the horse, and markedly greater in the camel and the llama than in the other two.

label: Height of vertebral spines is proportional to the local bending moment
statement: In the vertebral girder, ligaments form the upper tension member, vertebral bodies the lower compression member and the spines the web, and the height of the vertebral spines at each point along the back is proportional to the bending moment at that point.
quote: secondly we observe that the depth of the web, or distance apart of the principal members,—that is to say the height of the vertebral spines,—must be proportional to the bending-moment at each point along the length of the girder.
scope: vertebral columns of quadrupedal and bipedal vertebrates

label: Heavy heads give tall withers spines; heavy tails give tall lumbar-sacral spines
statement: Animals whose head and neck form a large fraction of body weight have large bending moments over the fore-legs and correspondingly tall spines over the withers, whereas animals with light heads and heavy tails (anteaters, Diplodocus) or that are bipedal (kangaroo, Iguanodon) have their tallest spines over the loins and haunches.
quote: Wherever we have a heavily loaded anterior cantilever arm, that is to say whenever the head and neck represent a considerable fraction of the whole weight of the body, we tend to have large bending-moments over the fore-legs, and correspondingly high spines over the vertebrae of the withers.
scope: terrestrial quadrupedal and bipedal vertebrates, living and fossil

label: Aquatic mammals lack the tall withers and haunch spines of land quadrupeds
statement: Because buoyancy neutralises gravity so that there are no piers or cantilevers, all aquatic mammals (whales, seals, sea-cows) have lost the high arched vertebral spines over the withers and haunches, and aquatic birds have a weak, straight pelvis compared with terrestrial birds.
quote: For here the effect of gravity is neutralised; we have neither piers nor cantilevers; and we find accordingly in all aquatic mammals of whatsoever group—whales, seals or sea-cows—that the high arched vertebral spines over the withers, or corresponding structures over the hind-limbs, have both entirely disappeared.
scope: aquatic mammals (cetaceans, pinnipeds, sirenians) and aquatic birds compared with terrestrial relatives

label: Fish vertebral processes are set at about 120° to one another for uniform stiffness
statement: In ordinary fishes such as cod and haddock (and partly in whales), the backbone is stiffened by three series of ligament-connected processes, dorsal and two transverse, arranged at nearly equal angles of 120°, which gives the greatest and most uniform strength possible for such a system.
quote: And here we see (as we see partly also among the whales), that these three series of processes, or struts, tend to be arranged well-nigh at equal angles, of 120°, with one another, giving the greatest and most uniform strength of which such a system is capable.
scope: vertebral columns of round-bodied fishes and cetaceans

label: Backbone girders are shallower than engineers would build because flexibility is needed
statement: The vertebral girder of large animals such as Diplodocus or Stegosaurus is shallower than an engineer's cantilever of comparable load, because a deeper girder would increase rigidity, and an animal's backbone must combine strength with flexibility.
quote: If we adopt a much greater depth (or ratio of depth to length) as in the modern cantilever, we shall greatly increase the _strength_ of the structure; but at the same time we should greatly increase its _rigidity_, and this is precisely what, in the circumstances of the case, it would seem that nature is bound to avoid.

label: Skeletal form is largely a diagram of mechanical stress
statement: Skeletal form, as produced by growth, is to a very large extent determined by mechanical stress: material is laid down along the lines of stress so as to avoid shear, from the trabeculae within each bone to the arrangement of the bones in the whole skeleton.
quote: Let us not press either argument or hypothesis too far: but be content to see that skeletal form, as brought about by growth, is to a very large extent determined by mechanical considerations, and tends to manifest itself as a diagram, or reflected image, of mechanical stress.
scope: vertebrate skeletons, from bone microstructure to whole-skeleton architecture

label: Mechanically shaped single bones are unreliable guides to phylogenetic affinity
statement: Because the form of bones such as the scapula or vertebrae reflects the mechanical stresses of an animal's mode of life, resemblance or difference in a single such bone is no reliable evidence for or against blood-relationship, as in comparing Zeuglodon with whales.
quote: That the Zeuglodon has a scapula like that of a whale is to my mind no necessary argument that he is akin by blood-relationship to a whale: that his dorsal vertebrae are very different from a whale’s is no conclusive argument that such blood-relationship is lacking.
scope: use of skeletal characters in vertebrate phylogenetics, especially in lineages that changed habitat

label: New mechanical forces modify many correlated parts together, not isolated bones
statement: When altered environment and habits introduce new forces, the resulting modifications of form appear not as isolated changes in single parts but as slow, general, graded modifications spread over many correlated parts or the whole body.
quote: And if this be really so, it will further imply that modifications of form will tend to manifest themselves, not so much in small and _isolated_ phenomena, in this part of the fabric or in that, in a scapula for instance or a humerus: but rather in some slow, _general_, and more or less uniform or graded modification, spread over a number of correlated parts
scope: evolutionary change of form in animals, especially skeletons

label: Organic forms depart from mathematical ideals only as inanimate forms do
statement: There is no essential difference between organic and inorganic form: living forms depart from ideal mathematical figures only because secondary forces act alongside the main one, just as no chain hangs as a perfect catenary and no raindrop is a perfect sphere.
quote: There is no such essential difference between these phenomena of organic form and those which are manifested in portions of inanimate matter. No chain hangs in a perfect catenary and no raindrop is a perfect sphere: and this for the simple reason that forces and resistances other than the main one are inevitably at work.

label: Specific differences in form are mainly differences of relative magnitude
statement: The essential differences in form between species of the same group are differences of proportion or relative magnitude (Aristotle's 'excess and defect'), and these are the main cause of specific differences.
quote: It is precisely this difference of relative magnitudes, this Aristotelian “excess and defect” in the case of form, which our co-ordinate method is especially adapted to analyse, and to reveal and demonstrate as the main cause of what (again in the Aristotelian sense) we term “specific” differences.
scope: species within the same zoological class or genus

label: Related organisms differ by simple, symmetrical Cartesian transformations
statement: The forms of related organisms can, as a general rule, be mapped onto one another by a simple and symmetrical deformation of a Cartesian coordinate grid, such as would result from a slight and simple change in the system of forces acting on the growing organism.
quote: We are dealing in this chapter with the forms of related organisms, in order to shew that the differences between them are as a general rule simple and symmetrical, and just such as might have been brought about by a slight and simple change in the system of forces to which the living and growing organism was exposed.
scope: related species within a zoological class (fishes, crustaceans, reptile and mammal skulls, etc.)

label: Evolutionary variation proceeds by correlated whole-body change, not character by character
statement: Because dissimilar related fishes can be referred as wholes to the same figure in different coordinate systems, variation has proceeded on definite and orderly lines under a comprehensive law of growth affecting the whole structure, rather than by independent variation of separate parts as the usual conception of natural selection assumes.
quote: But if, on the other hand, diverse and dissimilar fishes can be referred as a whole to identical functions of very different co-ordinate systems, this fact will of itself constitute a proof that variation has proceeded on definite and orderly lines, that a comprehensive “law of growth” has pervaded the whole structure in its integrity, and that some more or less simple and recognisable system of forces has been at work.
scope: evolutionary differentiation of related animal species

label: Shear-deformed fossils are often mistaken for distinct species
statement: Fossils in folded and inclined strata are often symmetrically deformed, usually by simple shear, so that they have been described as distinct species and occasionally even as new genera.
quote: the contained fossils are apt to be so curiously and yet so symmetrically deformed (usually by a simple shear) that they may easily be interpreted as so many distinct and separate “species.”

label: Cannon-bones of ox, sheep and giraffe differ by a simple one-axis stretch
statement: The cannon-bones of the ox, sheep and giraffe differ essentially only in relative length and breadth: at equal length, the sheep's bone is about two-thirds and the giraffe's about one-third as broad as the ox's.
quote: In other words, the main (and perhaps the only) difference between the two bones is simply that that of the sheep is elongated, along the vertical axis, as compared with that of the ox in the relation of 3/2.

label: Ratio of radial to tangential growth about a node yields lanceolate, ovate, cordate leaves
statement: Dicotyledon leaf shapes arise from growth radial to and transverse to radii about a node of no growth at the leaf base; increasing the ratio of tangential to radial growth carries the outline successively from lanceolate to ovate to cordate.
quote: If we now alter the ratio between the radial and tangential velocities of growth—in other words, if we increase the angles between corresponding radii—we pass successively through the various configurations which the botanist describes as the lanceolate, the ovate, and finally the cordate leaf.
scope: leaves of dicotyledons (contrasted with basally growing monocot leaves)

label: The lopsided begonia leaf reflects unequal, not asymmetrical, growth
statement: The two halves of a begonia leaf, one ovate and the other cordate, are mathematically similar figures produced by unequal growth on either side of the midrib, so that angles to equal radii on the two sides are in constant proportion.
quote: the so-called unsymmetrical leaf of a begonia, in which one side of the leaf may be merely ovate while the other has a cordate outline, is seen to be really a case of _unequal_, and not truly asymmetrical, growth on either side of the midrib.
